goals: Classify and name alcohols and compare 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols
Write equations to prepare alcohols from alkenes, Grignard reagents, alkyl halides, carbonyl compounds and primary amines
Outline the manufacture of methanol and ethanol
Explain the boiling points and solubility of alcohols

slides.heading: Alcohols
slides.body_md: Part 1 — compounds with an –OH group on an sp³ carbon: names, preparation and physical properties.

rows: Hand sanitiser, fuel blended with petrol

visual.alt: Table of familiar alcohols

slides.narration: Namaste! The sanitiser on your hands, the antifreeze in a car radiator and the glycerol in soap are all alcohols, compounds in which a hydroxyl group is attached to an sp three carbon. In this part we classify and name alcohols, learn several ways to make them, outline how methanol and ethanol are produced industrially, and see how hydrogen bonding controls their physical properties.

slides.heading: Classification and general formula
slides.body_md: By the number of –OH groups: **monohydric** (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH), **dihydric** (glycols), **trihydric** (glycerol). Monohydric alcohols are **primary**, **secondary** or **tertiary** according to the carbon bearing –OH.

visual.alt: Table classifying alcohols

slides.narration: Monohydric alcohols have one hydroxyl group and the general formula C n H two n plus one O H. Dihydric alcohols, or glycols, have two, and trihydric alcohols such as glycerol have three. Like haloalkanes, monohydric alcohols are primary, secondary or tertiary depending on how many carbons are bonded to the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group. The four butanol isomers show all three classes.

slides.heading: Nomenclature
slides.body_md: IUPAC: longest chain containing the C–OH; replace **-e** of the alkane by **-ol**; lowest locant to –OH. Diols and triols keep the **-e** (ethane-1,2-diol). Common names: alkyl + alcohol.

visual.alt: Table of common and IUPAC names of alcohols

slides.narration: To name an alcohol, find the longest chain containing the carbon with the hydroxyl group, number it to give that carbon the lowest number, and change the ending e of the alkane to ol. So isobutyl alcohol is two-methylpropan-one-ol and tert-butyl alcohol is two-methylpropan-two-ol. For diols the e is kept: ethylene glycol is ethane-one-two-diol.

slides.heading: Structure of the –OH group
slides.body_md: Oxygen is **sp³** hybridised with two lone pairs; the C–O–H angle in methanol (108.9°) is slightly less than tetrahedral because lone pairs repel more than bond pairs. The O–H bond is polar: H is δ+ and O is δ−.

slides.narration: In an alcohol the oxygen atom is sp three hybridised. Two of its hybrid orbitals form the bonds to carbon and hydrogen; the other two hold lone pairs. The lone pairs push the bonds slightly closer, so the carbon–oxygen–hydrogen angle is about one hundred and nine degrees, a little less than the tetrahedral value. The very polar O–H bond is the key to hydrogen bonding.

slides.heading: Worked example: naming and classifying
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name and classify: (a) $\ce{CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2OH}$; (b) $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH(OH)CH3}$; (c) $\ce{CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CH2CH3}$; (d) $\ce{HOCH2CH(OH)CH3}$.

**(a)** 2-Methylbutan-1-ol — primary.

**(b)** 3-Methylbutan-2-ol — secondary.

**(c)** 3-Methylpentan-3-ol — tertiary.

**(d)** Propane-1,2-diol — dihydric.

visual.alt: Flow for naming and classifying an alcohol

slides.narration: Number from the end nearer the hydroxyl group. In the first example the hydroxyl carbon is at the end of the chain with one carbon neighbour, so it is primary. In the second it has two carbon neighbours: secondary. In the third, the hydroxyl carbon has three ethyl or methyl groups: tertiary. The last has two hydroxyl groups, so it is a diol.

slides.heading: Preparation from alkenes
slides.body_md: **Direct hydration:** H₂O with H⁺ catalyst (Markovnikov). **Indirect hydration:** absorb the alkene in cold conc. H₂SO₄ to give an alkyl hydrogen sulphate, then boil with water. **Hydroboration–oxidation:** B₂H₆, then H₂O₂/OH⁻ — **anti-Markovnikov**, giving 1° alcohols from terminal alkenes.

visual.alt: Table of alcohols from alkenes

slides.narration: Water can be added across a double bond in three ways. Direct hydration with an acid catalyst and indirect hydration through an alkyl hydrogen sulphate both follow Markovnikov’s rule, putting the hydroxyl group on the more substituted carbon. Hydroboration followed by oxidation with alkaline hydrogen peroxide does the reverse, putting the hydroxyl group on the end carbon: but-one-ene gives butan-one-ol.

slides.heading: Other preparations
slides.body_md: **Hydrolysis of alkyl halides:** aqueous NaOH/KOH or moist Ag₂O. **Reduction of carbonyl compounds:** aldehydes → 1°, ketones → 2° (H₂/Ni, NaBH₄, LiAlH₄). **Primary amines with nitrous acid** (NaNO₂ + HCl): R–NH₂ → R–OH + N₂. **Grignard reagents:** HCHO → 1°; RCHO → 2°; R₂CO → 3°, after hydrolysis.

visual.alt: Table of Grignard routes to alcohols

slides.narration: Alcohols also come from alkyl halides boiled with aqueous alkali, from aldehydes and ketones by reduction, and from primary amines treated with nitrous acid, which releases nitrogen gas. Grignard reagents are especially useful because they build a new carbon–carbon bond: methanal gives primary alcohols, other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols.

slides.heading: Worked example: Grignard planning
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Choose a Grignard reagent and a carbonyl compound to make (a) ethanol, (b) propan-2-ol and (c) 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

**(a)** $\ce{CH3MgI}$ + methanal → $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$ (1°).

**(b)** $\ce{CH3MgI}$ + ethanal → $\ce{CH3CH(OH)CH3}$ (2°).

**(c)** $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr}$ + propanone → $\ce{CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)2}$ (3°) (or $\ce{CH3MgI}$ + butanone).

Each adduct is hydrolysed with dilute acid.

nodes.label: Cut one C–C bond at the carbinol carbon

visual.alt: Flow for planning a Grignard synthesis

slides.narration: Work backwards from the target. Look at the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group and cut one of its carbon–carbon bonds: the piece cut off becomes the Grignard reagent, and the rest, with the hydroxyl turned into a carbonyl group, is the carbonyl compound. For two-methylbutan-two-ol, cutting off the ethyl group leaves propanone, so ethylmagnesium bromide and propanone are needed.

slides.heading: Manufacture of methanol and ethanol (outline)
slides.body_md: **Methanol (Bosch process):** water gas (CO + H₂) from steam over hot coke, enriched with H₂, is passed over ZnO–Cr₂O₃ at about 573–673 K and 200–300 atm. **Ethanol (fermentation):** molasses (sucrose) or starch is fermented by yeast; invertase converts sucrose to glucose and fructose, zymase converts these to ethanol and CO₂ (about 8–10% ethanol).

visual.alt: Table outlining industrial manufacture of methanol and ethanol

slides.narration: Methanol is made from water gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen obtained by passing steam over red-hot coke. Extra hydrogen is added and the mixture is passed over zinc oxide and chromium three oxide at high temperature and pressure. Ethanol is made by fermentation: yeast enzymes convert the sucrose in molasses first into glucose and fructose, and then into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Physical properties: hydrogen bonding
slides.body_md: Alcohols are **associated by hydrogen bonds**, so they boil much higher than alkanes, ethers or haloalkanes of similar mass. B.p. rises with chain length and falls with branching (1° > 2° > 3° isomers). Lower alcohols are **miscible with water** (hydrogen bonding with water); solubility falls as the alkyl group grows.

slides.narration: Each hydroxyl hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair on the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. These hydrogen bonds must be broken when the alcohol boils, so alcohols boil far higher than hydrocarbons of similar mass. Methanol, ethanol and propanol mix with water in all proportions because they hydrogen-bond with water, but solubility falls as the hydrocarbon part becomes larger.

slides.heading: Worked example: boiling points
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange in increasing boiling point and explain: butan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, pentane, ethoxyethane (all $M \approx 72\text{–}74$).

**Step 1.** Pentane (309 K) and ethoxyethane (308 K): no O–H, no hydrogen bonding between molecules.

**Step 2.** The alcohols hydrogen-bond; branching lowers b.p.: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (356 K) < butan-1-ol (391 K).

**Order:** ethoxyethane ≈ pentane < 2-methylpropan-2-ol < butan-1-ol.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points of compounds of similar molar mass

slides.narration: All four have similar molar masses. Ethoxyethane and pentane cannot form hydrogen bonds between their molecules, so they boil lowest, near three hundred and eight kelvin. Both alcohols hydrogen-bond, so they boil much higher. Between them, the compact, branched two-methylpropan-two-ol has a smaller contact area than straight-chain butan-one-ol, so it boils lower.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Alcohols are classified by the number of hydroxyl groups and by the carbon carrying them, and named with the ending ol. They are made from alkenes, alkyl halides, carbonyl compounds, primary amines and Grignard reagents. Methanol comes from water gas and ethanol from fermentation. Hydrogen bonding gives alcohols high boiling points and makes the smaller ones soluble in water.

slides.heading: Reactions of alcohols
slides.body_md: Part 2 — reactions breaking the O–H bond, reactions breaking the C–O bond, oxidation, and tests.

nodes.label: C–O breaks: HX, PX₃, PCl₅, SOCl₂, dehydration

visual.alt: Flow classifying reactions of alcohols

slides.narration: Alcohol reactions fall into groups. Some break the oxygen–hydrogen bond, as with sodium and in ester formation. Others break the carbon–oxygen bond, as with hydrogen halides, phosphorus halides and thionyl chloride, or in dehydration. A third group oxidises the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group. In this part we study these, with the mechanisms of esterification and dehydration.

slides.heading: Acidic nature
slides.body_md: Alcohols react with active metals (Na, K) to give **alkoxides** and H₂, showing weak acidity. They are **weaker acids than water** because the alkyl group (+I) pushes electron density towards O, destabilising the alkoxide ion; alkoxides are strong bases. Acidity: CH₃OH > 1° > 2° > 3°.

visual.alt: Table of pKa values of water and alcohols

slides.narration: Sodium reacts with alcohols, releasing hydrogen and forming an alkoxide, so alcohols are weak acids. They are weaker even than water, because the alkyl group pushes electrons towards oxygen and makes the alkoxide ion less stable. That is why an alkoxide added to water takes a proton from it and gives back the alcohol and hydroxide. Bulkier alkyl groups make alcohols weaker acids still.

slides.heading: Replacement of –OH by halogen
slides.body_md: The C–O bond breaks. Reactivity with HX: **HI > HBr > HCl**; 3° > 2° > 1° (via carbocations). PCl₃, PCl₅ and SOCl₂ (best, gaseous by-products) also convert ROH to RCl.

visual.alt: Table of halogenating reagents and their by-products

slides.narration: Hydrogen halides replace the hydroxyl group by a halogen; hydrogen iodide reacts fastest and hydrogen chloride needs zinc chloride. Phosphorus trichloride and pentachloride also work; the white fumes of hydrogen chloride given off with phosphorus pentachloride are a test for a hydroxyl group. Thionyl chloride is best for a pure product, because both by-products are gases.

slides.heading: Esterification and acylation
slides.body_md: With a **carboxylic acid** and conc. H₂SO₄ (reversible) or with an **acid chloride** or **anhydride** (fast; pyridine removes HCl), the O–H hydrogen of the alcohol is replaced by an acyl group: an **ester** forms.

visual.alt: Table of acylating agents

slides.narration: Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form esters with fruity smells. The reaction is reversible, so water is removed or one reactant is used in excess. Acid chlorides and anhydrides react faster and completely; pyridine is added with acid chlorides to remove the hydrogen chloride formed.

slides.heading: Mechanism of acid-catalysed esterification
slides.body_md: (1) H⁺ **protonates the C=O oxygen** of the acid, making the carbon more electrophilic. (2) The alcohol oxygen **attacks** the carbonyl carbon (nucleophilic addition). (3) **Proton transfer** to an –OH group. (4) **Loss of water**. (5) **Loss of H⁺** gives the ester. Isotope labelling (¹⁸O in the alcohol) shows the ester oxygen comes from the **alcohol**: the acid loses –OH, the alcohol loses H.

visual.alt: Flow of the esterification mechanism

slides.narration: The acid catalyst first adds a proton to the carbonyl oxygen of the carboxylic acid, making its carbon more positive. The alcohol’s oxygen lone pair then attacks this carbon. After a proton moves onto one of the hydroxyl groups, water leaves, and finally a proton is lost to give the ester. Experiments with heavy oxygen in the alcohol show that it ends up in the ester, so the water comes from the acid.

slides.heading: Worked example: esters from alcohols
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the ester formed in each case: (a) propan-1-ol + ethanoic acid (H⁺); (b) methanol + ethanoyl chloride; (c) ethanol + ethanoic anhydride. If ethanol labelled with ¹⁸O reacts with ethanoic acid, where is the ¹⁸O found?

**(a)** Propyl ethanoate. **(b)** Methyl ethanoate. **(c)** Ethyl ethanoate (+ ethanoic acid).

**Label:** in the ester, $\ce{CH3CO-^{18}O-C2H5}$; the water formed contains ordinary oxygen.

visual.alt: Table of esters formed

slides.narration: Name an ester by giving the alkyl group from the alcohol first, then the acid part ending in oate. Propan-one-ol and ethanoic acid give propyl ethanoate; methanol and ethanoyl chloride give methyl ethanoate. With labelled oxygen in ethanol, the label ends up in the ester, because the alcohol supplies the oxygen that links the two parts, and the acid supplies the hydroxyl that leaves as water.

slides.heading: Oxidation of alcohols
slides.body_md: **1° alcohols** → aldehydes (PCC, or Cu at 573 K) → carboxylic acids (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄). **2° alcohols** → ketones. **3° alcohols** resist mild oxidation; over hot Cu they dehydrate to alkenes. With acidified dichromate, 1° and 2° alcohols turn the solution from orange to green.

visual.alt: Table of oxidation products

slides.narration: Oxidation removes hydrogen from the oxygen and from the carbon carrying it. A primary alcohol gives an aldehyde, and with excess strong oxidant goes on to a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on that carbon, so it resists mild oxidation; over hot copper it loses water instead and gives an alkene. These differences help identify the class of alcohol.

slides.heading: Dehydration: conditions and mechanism
slides.body_md: Ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄: **443 K → ethene**; **413 K** (excess alcohol) → ethoxyethane. Ease: 3° > 2° > 1°. **Mechanism:** (1) protonation of –OH: $\ce{CH3CH2OH + H+ -> CH3CH2OH2+}$; (2) loss of water to a carbocation: $\ce{CH3CH2OH2+ -> CH3CH2+ + H2O}$ (slow); (3) loss of H⁺ from the adjacent carbon: $\ce{CH3CH2+ -> CH2=CH2 + H+}$.

visual.alt: Flow of the dehydration mechanism

slides.narration: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes water from alcohols. With ethanol at four hundred and forty three kelvin, ethene forms; at four hundred and thirteen kelvin with excess ethanol, two molecules combine to give ethoxyethane. The acid first protonates the hydroxyl group, turning it into a good leaving group. Water leaves to give a carbocation, and a hydrogen ion is lost from the next carbon, forming the double bond. Tertiary alcohols dehydrate most easily.

slides.heading: Converting one alcohol into another
slides.body_md: **Ascent** (add one carbon): ROH → RCl (SOCl₂) → RMgCl (Mg, ether) → + HCHO, then H₃O⁺ → RCH₂OH. **Descent** (remove one carbon): RCH₂OH → RCOOH (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺) → RCONH₂ (NH₃, heat) → RNH₂ (Br₂ + KOH, Hofmann) → ROH (HNO₂).

visual.alt: Table of ascent and descent sequences

slides.narration: To go up the series by one carbon, turn the alcohol into a chloroalkane, make the Grignard reagent, and add methanal: hydrolysis gives the next higher primary alcohol. To go down, oxidise the alcohol to a carboxylic acid, convert it into an amide with ammonia, use the Hofmann bromamide reaction to lose one carbon as the amine, and treat the amine with nitrous acid to get the alcohol with one carbon fewer.

slides.heading: Worked example: ascent and descent
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) Convert ethanol into propan-1-ol. (b) Convert propan-1-ol into ethanol.

**(a)** $\ce{C2H5OH ->[SOCl2] C2H5Cl ->[Mg][dry ether] C2H5MgCl}$; + HCHO, then $\ce{H3O+}$ → $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$.

**(b)** (skeletal scheme, reagents over the arrows) $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH ->[K2Cr2O7/H+] CH3CH2COOH ->[NH3][\Delta] CH3CH2CONH2 ->[Br2/KOH] CH3CH2NH2 ->[HNO2] CH3CH2OH}$.

slides.narration: For the ascent, ethanol becomes chloroethane, then ethylmagnesium chloride; adding methanal and hydrolysing gives propan-one-ol, one carbon longer. For the descent, propan-one-ol is oxidised to propanoic acid, converted into propanamide, and the Hofmann reaction removes one carbon to give ethanamine. Nitrous acid then converts ethanamine into ethanol.

slides.heading: Lucas test; uses of methanol and ethanol
slides.body_md: **Lucas reagent** (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl₂) at room temperature: **3°** turbid at once; **2°** in about 5 minutes; **1°** no turbidity (only on heating) — the insoluble chloroalkane forms fastest from the most stable carbocation.

Solvent, sanitisers, medicines, beverages, fuel (blended with petrol)

slides.narration: The Lucas test distinguishes the three classes. Shake the alcohol with concentrated hydrochloric acid and zinc chloride at room temperature. A tertiary alcohol turns cloudy immediately as the insoluble chloroalkane separates; a secondary one in about five minutes; a primary one stays clear. Methanol is a useful solvent and fuel but is very poisonous, while ethanol is used in medicines, sanitisers and as a petrol additive.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Alcohols are weak acids, weaker than water. Their hydroxyl group can be replaced by halogens or acylated to give esters by a mechanism in which the alcohol oxygen attacks the protonated acid. Oxidation and the Lucas test distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and acid dehydration gives alkenes or ethers. Alcohols can be stepped up or down the series by known sequences.

sections.heading: 2. Preparation
sections.body_md:
- **Alkenes:** direct hydration (H₂O/H⁺) or indirect (cold conc. H₂SO₄ then boil with water) — Markovnikov; **hydroboration–oxidation** (B₂H₆; H₂O₂/OH⁻) — anti-Markovnikov.
- **Alkyl halides:** aqueous KOH or moist Ag₂O.
- **Carbonyl reduction:** aldehyde → 1°, ketone → 2° (H₂/Ni, NaBH₄, LiAlH₄); esters/acids → 1° (LiAlH₄).
- **Primary amines + HNO₂:** RNH₂ → ROH + N₂ + H₂O.
- **Grignard:** HCHO → 1°; RCHO → 2°; R₂CO → 3° (then H₃O⁺).

key_terms.definition_md: Addition of B₂H₆ to an alkene followed by H₂O₂/OH⁻; gives anti-Markovnikov alcohols.

formulas.label: Grignard addition to methanal (then H₃O⁺ gives ethanol)

sections.heading: 3. Manufacture (outline)
sections.body_md:
**Methanol (Bosch):** $\ce{C + H2O -> CO + H2}$ (water gas, 1273 K); $\ce{CO + 2H2 -> CH3OH}$ over ZnO–Cr₂O₃, 573–673 K, 200–300 atm.
**Ethanol (fermentation):** molasses (sucrose) + yeast; invertase: sucrose → glucose + fructose; zymase: $\ce{C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Yeast enzyme complex converting glucose into ethanol and CO₂.
A mixture of CO and H₂ made from steam and hot coke.

visual.alt: Table of manufacture

sections.heading: 4. Acidity and reactions of the O–H and C–O bonds
sections.body_md:
**Acidity:** 2ROH + 2Na → 2RONa + H₂; alcohols are weaker acids than water (+I of alkyl); CH₃OH > 1° > 2° > 3°.

**C–O cleavage:** HX (HI > HBr > HCl; ZnCl₂ for HCl); PCl₃, PCl₅ (white HCl fumes — test for –OH); SOCl₂ (gaseous by-products).

**Esterification:** RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄); acid chlorides (pyridine) and anhydrides give esters irreversibly. **Mechanism:** protonate acid C=O → alcohol O attacks → proton transfer → lose H₂O → lose H⁺; ester O comes from the alcohol.

key_terms.definition_md: Formation of an ester from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid (or acid chloride/anhydride).

visual.alt: Table of reactions of alcohols

sections.heading: 5. Oxidation and dehydration
sections.body_md:
**Oxidation:** 1° → aldehyde (PCC; Cu, 573 K) → acid (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, KMnO₄); 2° → ketone; 3° resist (Cu, 573 K → alkene). Dichromate turns orange → green with 1° and 2°.

**Dehydration (conc. H₂SO₄):** ethanol → ethene at 443 K; → ethoxyethane at 413 K (excess ethanol). Ease 3° > 2° > 1°. **Mechanism:** $\ce{CH3CH2OH + H+ -> CH3CH2OH2+}$; $\ce{CH3CH2OH2+ -> CH3CH2+ + H2O}$ (slow); $\ce{CH3CH2+ -> CH2=CH2 + H+}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Pyridinium chlorochromate, a mild oxidant that converts 1° alcohols into aldehydes.

visual.alt: Table of oxidation products

sections.heading: 6. Conversions, Lucas test and uses
sections.body_md:
**Ascent:** ROH → RCl → RMgCl → + HCHO, H₃O⁺ → RCH₂OH. **Descent:** RCH₂OH → RCOOH → RCONH₂ → RNH₂ (Br₂/KOH, Hofmann) → ROH (HNO₂).

**Lucas test** (anhydrous ZnCl₂ + conc. HCl, room temperature): 3° turbid at once; 2° about 5 min; 1° no turbidity.

**Uses:** methanol — solvent, methanal manufacture, fuel; highly poisonous. Ethanol — solvent, medicines, sanitisers, beverages, fuel blended with petrol.

key_terms.definition_md: Anhydrous ZnCl₂ in conc. HCl, used to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
RCONH₂ + Br₂ + KOH → RNH₂ with one carbon fewer.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying alcohols are stronger acids than water.
- Placing the ¹⁸O label in the water during esterification (it stays in the ester).
- Forgetting temperatures for dehydration (443 K ethene; 413 K ether).
- Grignard + HCHO giving 2° alcohols (it gives 1°).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Mechanisms (2–3 marks): every step with the intermediate.
- Conversions (1 mark per step): reagent and intermediate.
- Tests (1–2 marks): reagent and observation for each class.

options.text_md: one primary and one secondary –OH group
one secondary and one tertiary –OH group

questions.solution_md: C-1 (CH₂OH) is primary; C-2 (CHOH) is secondary — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The general formula of the saturated, open-chain monohydric alcohols is:
questions.solution_md: CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH = CₙH₂ₙ₊₂O — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Propan-1-ol, methoxyethane and butane have similar molar masses (58–60). Which has the highest boiling point, and why?

options.text_md: Propan-1-ol, because its molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another
Methoxyethane, because it is the most polar
Butane, because it has the most hydrogen atoms
All boil at about the same temperature

questions.solution_md: Only the alcohol has an O–H group for intermolecular hydrogen bonding — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but butan-1-ol is only partly soluble. The reason is that in butan-1-ol:

options.text_md: the –OH group cannot form hydrogen bonds
the larger hydrocarbon part cannot hydrogen-bond with water
the oxygen has no lone pairs

questions.solution_md: The non-polar alkyl chain disrupts water’s hydrogen bonding — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol are functional group isomers.
questions.solution_md: False. Both are alcohols; they are chain/position isomers. A functional isomer would be an ether such as ethoxyethane.

questions.stem_md: The number of structural isomers of C₄H₉OH that are alcohols is ___.
questions.solution_md: **4**: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

questions.stem_md: Match each alcohol with its class.
questions.solution_md: Butan-1-ol 1°; butan-2-ol 2°; 2-methylpropan-2-ol 3°; ethane-1,2-diol dihydric.

questions.stem_md: Write the structures of (a) 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol and (b) 2-methylbutan-2-ol, and classify each alcohol.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) (CH₃)₃CCH₂OH — primary (the C–OH carbon has one C neighbour). (b) CH₃CH₂C(OH)(CH₃)₂ — tertiary.

questions.stem_md: Butan-1-ol boils at 391 K but its isomer 2-methylpropan-2-ol boils at 356 K. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Both form hydrogen bonds, but 2-methylpropan-2-ol is highly branched and nearly spherical; its smaller surface area gives weaker van der Waals forces and the bulky groups around –OH hinder hydrogen bonding. The unbranched butan-1-ol has stronger intermolecular attractions and boils higher.

questions.solution_md: Branching reduces surface area and hinders H-bonding.

questions.stem_md: Write the structures and IUPAC names of the four alcohols with formula C₄H₁₀O, and classify each as primary, secondary or tertiary.

answer.model_answer_md: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH, butan-1-ol (1°); CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, butan-2-ol (2°); (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH, 2-methylpropan-1-ol (1°); (CH₃)₃COH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°).

questions.solution_md: Four alcohols: 1°, 2°, 1°, 3°.

questions.solution_md: Indirect hydration follows Markovnikov’s rule — option (d).

questions.solution_md: Hydroboration–oxidation is anti-Markovnikov: –OH on the CH₂ end — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Propanal is reduced with hydrogen over nickel. The product is:
questions.solution_md: Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Ethanamine is treated with sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid in the cold. The organic product and the gas evolved are:
questions.solution_md: C₂H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ → C₂H₅OH + N₂ + H₂O — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Ketone + RMgX → tertiary alcohol — option (a).

questions.solution_md: Moist Ag₂O acts as a source of OH⁻ — option (d).

ethoxide is a weaker base than hydroxide
ethanol is a weaker acid than water

questions.solution_md: The stronger base (ethoxide) takes a proton from the stronger acid (water) — option (d).

questions.solution_md: More alkyl groups (+I) destabilise the alkoxide more — option (d).

questions.solution_md: ROH + PCl₅ → RCl + POCl₃ + HCl — option (c).

questions.solution_md: Acid strength and nucleophilicity of X⁻ increase from Cl to I — option (c).

options.text_md: shared equally between ester and water

questions.solution_md: (CH₃CO)₂O + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + CH₃COOH — option (c).

Choose the correct option.

questions.solution_md: Sodium **ethoxide**, C₂H₅ONa.

questions.solution_md: $n(\text{ester}) = 0.50 \times 0.67 = 0.335\ \text{mol}$; mass $= 0.335 \times 88 = 29.48\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: Arrange water, methanol, ethanol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol in order of increasing acid strength, and explain the order.

answer.model_answer_md: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol < ethanol < methanol ≈ water (water slightly stronger than ethanol; methanol about equal to water). Alkyl groups release electrons (+I), increasing negative charge on the alkoxide oxygen and destabilising the ion; the more alkyl groups, the weaker the acid. Bulky groups also hinder solvation of the alkoxide.

questions.stem_md: Give the mechanism of the acid-catalysed esterification of ethanoic acid with ethanol.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) H⁺ protonates the carbonyl oxygen of CH₃COOH, making the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic. (2) The lone pair on the ethanol oxygen attacks this carbon, giving a tetrahedral intermediate. (3) A proton is transferred to one of the –OH groups. (4) Water leaves, regenerating C=O (protonated). (5) Loss of H⁺ gives ethyl ethanoate and regenerates the catalyst.

questions.solution_md: Protonation; attack; proton transfer; loss of water; loss of H⁺.

marking_scheme.step: Proton transfer and loss of water

questions.stem_md: Write equations for the reaction of ethanol with (a) ethanoyl chloride, (b) ethanoic anhydride and (c) phosphorus pentachloride, naming the organic products.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $\ce{CH3COCl + C2H5OH -> CH3COOC2H5 + HCl}$: ethyl ethanoate. (b) $\ce{(CH3CO)2O + C2H5OH -> CH3COOC2H5 + CH3COOH}$: ethyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid. (c) $\ce{C2H5OH + PCl5 -> C2H5Cl + POCl3 + HCl}$: chloroethane.

questions.stem_md: Explain why ethanol heated with conc. H₂SO₄ gives ethene at 443 K but ethoxyethane at 413 K when ethanol is in excess.

answer.model_answer_md: At 413 K with excess ethanol, a second ethanol molecule attacks the protonated alcohol (substitution, SN2), giving the ether: intermolecular dehydration. At the higher temperature, 443 K, elimination is favoured: the protonated alcohol loses water and H⁺ to form ethene (intramolecular dehydration).

questions.solution_md: Substitution at lower T with excess alcohol; elimination at higher T.

questions.stem_md: Give the three steps of the mechanism of the acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Protonation: $\ce{CH3CH2OH + H+ -> CH3CH2OH2+}$ (fast). (2) Loss of water to give the ethyl carbocation: $\ce{CH3CH2OH2+ -> CH3CH2+ + H2O}$ (slow). (3) Loss of H⁺ from the adjacent carbon: $\ce{CH3CH2+ -> CH2=CH2 + H+}$; the catalyst is regenerated.

questions.solution_md: Protonation; loss of water; loss of H⁺.

questions.stem_md: Describe the Lucas test and state the observations for pentan-1-ol, pentan-2-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

answer.model_answer_md: The alcohol is shaken with Lucas reagent (anhydrous ZnCl₂ in conc. HCl) at room temperature; a chloroalkane forms, which is insoluble and makes the solution cloudy. 2-Methylbutan-2-ol (3°): cloudy at once. Pentan-2-ol (2°): cloudy in about 5 minutes. questions.stem_md: Show how propan-1-ol can be converted into butan-1-ol, giving the reagent for each step.

questions.stem_md: Show how ethanol can be converted into methanol, giving reagents and the name of each intermediate.

answer.model_answer_md: Oxidise with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: ethanoic acid. Heat with NH₃ (via ammonium ethanoate): ethanamide, $\ce{CH3CONH2}$. Br₂ + KOH (Hofmann bromamide): methanamine, $\ce{CH3NH2}$. NaNO₂ + HCl (HNO₂): methanol.

questions.solution_md: Acid → amide → amine → alcohol.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Show how propene can be converted into (i) propan-2-ol and (ii) propan-1-ol, naming the rule each method follows. [2]

(b) Choose a Grignard reagent and a carbonyl compound to prepare 3-methylpentan-3-ol, and write the equations. [1½]

(c) Outline the manufacture of methanol, with equations. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) $\ce{CH3CH=CH2 + H2O ->[H+] CH3CH(OH)CH3}$ (or via H₂SO₄, then water) — Markovnikov. (ii) $\ce{CH3CH=CH2 ->[(i) B2H6][(ii) H2O2/OH-] CH3CH2CH2OH}$ — anti-Markovnikov.

(b) Ethylmagnesium bromide with butanone: $\ce{CH3CH2MgBr + CH3COCH2CH3 -> (CH3CH2)2C(CH3)OMgBr}$; hydrolysis with dilute acid gives $\ce{(CH3CH2)2C(OH)CH3}$, 3-methylpentan-3-ol.

(c) $\ce{C + H2O -> CO + H2}$ (water gas); $\ce{CO + 2H2 ->[ZnO-Cr2O3][573-673 K, 200-300 atm] CH3OH}$.

questions.solution_md: Hydration vs hydroboration; EtMgBr + butanone; Bosch.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why alcohols are weaker acids than water, and write the equation for the reaction of propan-1-ol with sodium. [1½]

(b) Give the mechanism of the acid-catalysed reaction between ethanoic acid and ethanol. [2]

(c) Compare the reactions of ethanol with PCl₅ and with SOCl₂, and state which is preferred for preparing chloroethane and why. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The alkyl group releases electrons (+I), destabilising the alkoxide ion, so the alcohol loses H⁺ less readily than water. $\ce{2CH3CH2CH2OH + 2Na -> 2CH3CH2CH2ONa + H2}$.

(b) Protonation of the acid C=O; attack by the ethanol oxygen on the carbonyl carbon; proton transfer; loss of water; loss of H⁺ to give ethyl ethanoate.

(c) $\ce{C2H5OH + PCl5 -> C2H5Cl + POCl3 + HCl}$; $\ce{C2H5OH + SOCl2 -> C2H5Cl + SO2 + HCl}$. SOCl₂ is preferred: its by-products are gases and escape, leaving pure chloroethane, whereas POCl₃ (liquid) must be separated.

questions.solution_md: +I effect; ester mechanism; SOCl₂ preferred.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Three isomeric alcohols P, Q and R have the formula C₄H₁₀O. With acidified dichromate, P gives an aldehyde and then an acid, Q gives a ketone and R is not oxidised. Suggest structures for P, Q and R and name the oxidation products of P and Q. [2]

(b) Give the mechanism of the acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene. [2]

(c) What is formed when ethanol is heated with conc. H₂SO₄ at 413 K? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) P: butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH (or 2-methylpropan-1-ol) → butanal → butanoic acid. Q: butan-2-ol, CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ → butanone. R: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH₃)₃COH (tertiary, no H on the carbinol carbon).

(b) $\ce{CH3CH2OH + H+ -> CH3CH2OH2+}$; $\ce{CH3CH2OH2+ -> CH3CH2+ + H2O}$ (slow); $\ce{CH3CH2+ -> CH2=CH2 + H+}$.

(c) Ethoxyethane (diethyl ether), $\ce{C2H5OC2H5}$, with ethanol in excess.

questions.solution_md: P 1°, Q 2°, R 3°; three-step mechanism; ether.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Show how methanol can be converted into ethanol. [2]

(b) Show how propan-1-ol can be converted into ethanol. [2]

(c) How would you distinguish propan-2-ol from 2-methylpropan-2-ol by the Lucas test? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{CH3OH ->[SOCl2] CH3Cl ->[Mg][dry ether] CH3MgCl}$; + HCHO, then dilute acid → $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$.

(b) $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH ->[K2Cr2O7/H+] CH3CH2COOH ->[NH3][\Delta] CH3CH2CONH2 ->[Br2/KOH] CH3CH2NH2 ->[HNO2] CH3CH2OH}$.

(c) With Lucas reagent at room temperature, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°) turns cloudy at once; propan-2-ol (2°) takes about 5 minutes.

questions.solution_md: Ascent via Grignard; descent via Hofmann; Lucas.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations for the production of ethanol from sucrose by fermentation, naming the enzymes. [2]

(b) Give two uses of methanol and explain why it must never be drunk. [1½]

(c) Give a chemical test to distinguish ethanol from methanol. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[invertase] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$ (glucose + fructose); $\ce{C6H12O6 ->[zymase] 2C2H5OH + 2CO2}$.

(b) Uses: solvent for paints and varnishes; manufacture of methanal; fuel. It is very poisonous: it is oxidised in the body to methanal and methanoic acid, causing blindness and death.

(c) Iodoform test: warm with I₂ and NaOH; ethanol gives a yellow precipitate of CHI₃, methanol does not.

questions.solution_md: Invertase, zymase; uses and toxicity; iodoform test.
